811.quote_or_event: “Our intimacy with those to whom we are not bound by the chain of f'riendship, O king of the hills, the sides of which are covered with groves of tall sandal-trees! though it seem day by day to increase, will be dissolved as instantaneously as fire catches straw.”
811.explanation: The poet warns that an intimacy not grounded in real friendship may seem to grow day by day, yet it vanishes as fast as straw catches fire.
811.tie_back: The Kural says it is sweeter for the effusive friendship of people of poor character to shrink than to grow, and the Naladiyar likewise sees no value in such growing intimacy, since it will burn away at once.
811.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
811._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text, including the source's typo "f'riendship". Tamil Jain didactic verse; it shares the idea of distrusting a show of growing intimacy, but it predicts that such a bond will collapse rather than saying it is better for it to shrink.

812.quote_or_event: “men will remain until they have done their work in an old house the thatch of which is untied, keeping out the water br a dam, and being drenched with the rain falling down upon them. Thus will friends! remain with one until their business is finished.”
812.explanation: The poet compares self-serving friends to men who put up with a leaking old house only until their work there is finished, and then leave.
812.tie_back: The Kural describes the unworthy who befriend you while there is gain and leave when it ends, and the Naladiyar's friends who stay only until their business is done describe the same thing.
812.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
812._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text; 'br' and 'friends!' are printed that way in the source, and the opening vocative is left out. Tamil Jain didactic verse; a near one-to-one match for friendship that lasts only as long as it pays.

813.quote_or_event: “If you impartially investigate the two things, it will be found that there is no difference between the shining light of a lamp and the love of courtesans. When the oil is exhausted, the light of the lamp vanishes, and when the money of their lovers is gone, their love also evaporates.”
813.explanation: The poet compares mercenary affection to a lamp that shines only while there is oil, so that the love ends as soon as the money runs out.
813.tie_back: The Kural puts the calculating friend on a level with those who love only for what they receive, whom the commentators identify as courtesans, and the Naladiyar's lamp image shows exactly that love which lasts only as long as the payment.
813.source: Naladiyar, ch. 38 'Courtesans', stanza 1 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
813._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text. Tamil Jain didactic verse; it matches only the middle figure of the Kural's three and says nothing about the friend who weighs his gain or about the thief.

814.quote_or_event: “If he does not meet with a clever companion who surpasses or equals him in virtue, he should live by himself, abstaining from sins and not devoted to pleasures.”
814.explanation: The Jain canon tells the monk to choose a companion at least his equal in virtue, and to live alone if none can be found.
814.tie_back: The Kural says it is better to be alone than to have companions who, like an untrained horse, throw you in the midst of battle, and the Uttaradhyayana likewise prefers solitude to an unworthy companion.
814.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
814._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on the sacred-texts.com archive. Canonical and a close fit for 'better alone than badly accompanied', though the context is a monk's spiritual companion and the Kural's image of betrayal in battle has no counterpart.

815.quote_or_event: “The friendship of illustrious men is eminently valuable, and is productive of benefit as timely rain. But the f'riendship of the mean, even in the time of their prosperity, resembles, O lord of the land of clear water! the failure of rain in its due season.”
815.explanation: The poet contrasts the friendship of noble people, which helps like timely rain, with the friendship of the mean, which fails you like rain that does not come when it is due.
815.tie_back: The Kural calls the friendship of small-minded people who will not protect you, even when you have done everything for them, better never gained, and the Naladiyar likewise says the friendship of the mean fails when it is most needed.
815.source: Naladiyar, ch. 24 'Improper Friendship', stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
815._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text, including the source's typo "f'riendship". Tamil Jain didactic verse; it shares the theme that mean friends fail you, but not the Kural's point that such friendship is better never gained.

816.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.”
816.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana names avoiding foolish people, together with serving one's teachers and study, as part of the road to liberation.
816.tie_back: The Kural ranks even distance from the wise far above close friendship with a fool, and the Jain canon likewise makes keeping away from fools part of the path itself.
816.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
816._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on the sacred-texts.com archive. Canonical and on the same theme of shunning fools, but it has no counterpart to the Kural's striking comparison with being a stranger, or even an opponent, to the wise.

817.quote_or_event: “It is better to be without the love of those who are without sincerity. Death is preferable to an incurable disease. To kill him at once is more desirable than to vex a man so that he becomes sore at heart, and to abuse is better than to praise one for that which we do not possess.”
817.explanation: In a string of 'better than' sayings, the poet holds that it is better to have no love at all than insincere love, and better to be abused than falsely praised.
817.tie_back: The Kural says what comes from enemies is worth far more than the friendship of those who only laugh along with you, and the Naladiyar likewise prefers open hostility to hollow affection and flattery.
817.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 9 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
817._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text. Tamil Jain didactic verse; its 'better than' pattern and its contrast of insincere love with outright abuse are close to the Kural's, though the laughing companion is not named.

818.quote_or_event: “Though they adhere to one in friendship as closely as the small toes of a dog to one another, yet of what benefit is the love of those who do not help one even to the extent of the leg of a fly?”
818.explanation: The poet asks what use there is in the love of friends who cling closely yet will not help even in the smallest way.
818.tie_back: The Kural tells us to let friendship quietly slacken with those who spoil a task they could easily do, and the Naladiyar likewise questions the worth of close friends who will not lift a finger to help.
818.source: Naladiyar, ch. 22 'The choice of friends', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
818._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the wisdomlib.org text (first sentence of the stanza). Tamil Jain didactic verse; it matches the unhelpful friend but has no counterpart to the Kural's specific advice to let the friendship fade quietly, without announcing a break.

819.quote_or_event: “माया मित्ताणि नासेइ” (māyā mittāṇi nāsei), “Deception destroys friendship”
819.explanation: The Dasavaikalika names deceit (maya), one of the four passions (kashayas) that bind karma to the soul, as the passion that specifically destroys friendship.
819.tie_back: The Kural says friendship with people whose deeds differ from their words is painful even in a dream, and the Jain canon names this kind of double-dealing as the very thing that destroys friendship.
819.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.38, Prakrit text with English rendering on tattvagyan.com ('Destroyer of friends')
819._accuracy_note: The Prakrit line and its English rendering were checked word for word on tattvagyan.com, a Jain devotional site rather than a scholarly translation. Canonical, but it treats deceit in general rather than the specific gap between word and deed, and has nothing like the Kural's 'even in a dream'.

820.quote_or_event: “If he is frequently angry; if he perseveres in his wrath; if he spurns friendly advice; if he is proud of his learning; if he finds fault with others; if he is angry even with friends; if he speaks evil even of a good friend behind his back … then he is called ill-behaved.”
820.explanation: Among the faults that mark a monk as ill-behaved and keep him from Nirvana, the Uttaradhyayana lists speaking evil of a good friend behind his back.
820.tie_back: The Kural warns against coming even slightly close to those who are friendly at home but run you down in public, and the Jain canon condemns that same two-faced disparaging of a friend as a fault that blocks liberation.
820.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.7–9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
820._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com, with the rest of the list left out at the ellipsis. Canonical and squarely on the fault of speaking ill of a friend behind his back, but it condemns the fault in oneself rather than advising wariness of such friends.
